comments.author: @Urgelt
comments.text:
99% of people working on movies are not artists. Not creative. They fit into a workflow and draw their livings from it. But if you sit them down to talk about their artistic vision, there isn't one.

Those are the workers who are most threatened by SORA. It's a lot of people.

Real creatives are uncommon. So uncommon, some movies are made without any at all, I would say. Nothing original occurs to them. Formulaic. Mechanistic. Imitative. Bureaucratic.

They are needed in the current paradigm, of course. Vision alone does not put movies in front of eyeballs.

But SORA flips the script. Or it appears that it will, as it gets better. A single creative in a basement somewhere could produce a very compelling film.

Probably. In truth, it has not yet happened. But it looks like it will.

I see this as a win for creatives, and a big win for consumers, but a big loss for everyone else in the industry.

As AI proceeds, jobs will be destroyed. Tax revenues will collapse at the very time our need for a social safety net accelerates. That is our biggest problem.

Our current economic models have no answers.

comments.author: @NikoKun
comments.text: A UBI is likely going to be what most people will support, once they realize what's coming, but at the moment it's also the most misunderstood idea.. For the reasons you state, I think people need to be made aware that a UBI is supposed be setup as an "*Unconditional* Basic Income", without such qualifiers on receiving it. And in the context we're discussing, it should also be setup as an AI Dividend for all, which scales with the economic growth from AI. We need to demand that it be truly unconditional, for all, and specifically implemented to fairly distribute the benefits of AI and ever increasing automation, to everyone. There's no reason to come up with another confusing plan by a different name.

comments.author: @amsrremix2239
comments.text:
I work as salaried 3D artist. The thing is- we’re ALREADY there. ComfyUI is almost professional. Completely nodes base OS. Which is how professionals work… however you still need to have a basic concept of making passes , understand how you can make textures and input them in your model….

People waiting for it to get dumbed down even more don’t realize it’s already as high level as it can be . Meaning - it can’t get any simpler- literally it can’t get simpler that just pressing a button to generate something…

However when you look on Hugging Face / Comfy UI etc etc… the people doing cool stuff still understand art.

Because they understand masking , ambient occlusion, normal maps they are you using it in an advanced way.

You STILL have to understand the underlying tech before you can make advanced stuff. 

Hopefully that makes sense . To sum it up. One button click will NEVER be the end goal. If you want control over your generations you still need knowledge on depth maps , masking etc… and node work flows. At least that how people are using it in pro sense right now

comments.author: @bishnooktawak
comments.text: About the economic models, I don't really see how any company could be doing great in a society plagued with mass unemployment. I've been thinking very superficially about the question of AI's socioeconomic disruptions and never really had time to dig into it seriously but, from what I see from those who talk about it, I feel like they're often forgetting to factor in some fundamental variables, e.g. the cost and availability of resources necessary to run AI and automation on such a massive scale (often inferred in such scenarios to remain as readily available and cheap - if not cheaper - than it is today, but that seems overly optimistic and simplistic to me) or, if goods do become extremely cheap, how that squares with a logic of supply and demand in this framework, that is to say with an actual market - which seems to me like a requirement to be able to say that any given company is "doing great." I rarely see any concern about global warming and other environmental issues either, when unhindered development of AI and robotics is bound to make them much, much more severe very fast - unless of course you're betting on nuclear fusion and/or AGI to fix them for us, which is all but a good idea at this stage. So, yeah, not convinced that any of these takes are thoroughly addressing the issues at hand...

comments.author: @synsam12345
comments.text:
11:20 - It's actually this person that's the misguided one. I too have worked many years in the industry, mainly for the big boi companies. If you know your history you know technical advancements has improved the indie scene. Just take the French New Wave as an example, shedding light on new directors like Jean-Luc Godard or Truffaut. Previously, cameras were huge and big, so you needed a big studio setup for them. Then the handheld camera came out. All of the sudden people could run around on real streets (not fake streets built at a studio for a lot of money) and through that indie film was revolutionized. Same with when the digital camera came out, just look at how that helped the shooting of 28 days later, a zombie flick. Due to the easier setups, they only had to shut down famous streets for a very short time to shoot their clips. Usually, filming on famous streets are super difficult. But due to the ease of digital filmmaking, they could make it work.

People will claim over and over that new technology will harm the industry, but from an art historical viewpoint they have always been wrong. It's like when people claimed the internet would kill art. These people make a big fuzz but in the end they always lose.

Certainly, the world is about to significantly change in the next 3-10 years as AI systems become more and more capable.  However, companies can't flourish without income and who provides that income--consumers, or rather, people.  If Sam Altman, Bill Gates or Elon Musk create just a few mega-corporations that can provide every AI service that humans are capable of, someone needs to be able to pay for those services.  If we eliminate 99% of that work, leaving 99% of the population unemployed, then there's next to no one left to pay for it.

Instead, what we will see that as the capability of AI increases, we will see careers pivot.  New markets that kill one form of labor always open up new forms of other types of labor.  Some times the skills in the old market do not map directly to the new market, but the net increase is often the need for more workers, and not fewer.  It's disruptive, yes, but we've not yet found a way to alleviate the need for work. In fact, some historians even estimate that we work harder today than many people have historically.  They may have been a bit poorer, but they had far more leisure time.  I don't know what they will look like but something tells me that as AI becomes more and more ubiquitous, new forms of "human" jobs will reveal themselves and they will be quite necessary.
